title: Tiger Woods to return to competitive golf next month for Hero World Challenge
content:
For the first time since his DUI arrest in March, Tiger Woods is returning to competitive golf.

Woods will compete in the Hero World Challenge, hosted in Albany, Bahamas, from Dec. 3-6. Woods, Gary Woodland and Rickie Fowler join as exemptions, rounding out the field, the Hero World Challenge announced Tuesday. It will be Woods’ first tournament since the 2024 Open Championship.

Woods organizes the Bahamas tournament annually for 20 of the world’s best PGA Tour players. Scottie Scheffler, Justin Thomas and Cameron Young are among the top names participating this year.

Woods has been largely out of the public eye since he clipped a pickup truck in his neighborhood in Jupiter, Fla., on March 27, causing his car to roll over.

As a result of the accident, the 15-time major champion was charged with driving under the influence with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful urinalysis. Neither Woods nor the driver of the truck reported injuries from the crash, and Woods was arrested after he failed a sobriety test. Officers at the scene described Woods as “lethargic,” and two hydrocodone pills were later found in Woods’ pocket, according to an arrest affidavit released by the Martin County Sheriff’s Office.

Woods reached a plea deal in early September to avoid jail time, with multiple charges reduced. His DUI charge was reduced to a reckless driving charge, second offense. The other charge — refusal to submit to a lawful urinalysis — was also reduced.

The motivation for a plea deal came due to a “significant erosion” of evidence, as toxicologists hired by Woods’ attorney and the state of Florida independently concluded that his long history of treating injuries with painkillers had created a pharmacological tolerance.

As part of the deal, Woods’ driver’s license was suspended for five years. Breaking the terms carries the penalty of jail.

Shortly after the accident, Woods announced he would be “stepping away” for an undisclosed period of time to “seek treatment.” The court permitted him to leave the country to spend several weeks at a rehabilitation facility in Switzerland.

“This is necessary in order for me to prioritize my well-being and work toward lasting recovery,” Woods said in a statement. “I’m committed to taking the time needed to return in a healthier, stronger and more focused place, both personally and professionally.”

It was not the first time Woods has stepped away from the public eye to seek treatment. In 2009, he spent 45 days in an inpatient clinic after news of multiple affairs came to light, shocking the sports world. After a DUI arrest in 2017, Woods completed a private intensive program to address his sleep disorder and pain management for his numerous back injuries.

One of Woods’ only public appearances since his court date came in June during a PGA Tour news conference, when he helped announce the tour’s competitive overhaul. Another came last week when he attended an event to celebrate his son Charlie signing to play at Florida State.

Woods served as the chairman of the Future Competition Committee both before and after the accident, taking a brief leave of absence from his boardroom duties before returning to the position.

The last time Woods swung a golf club on TV was three days before his arrest in March, during the finals of TGL, the simulator golf league he co-founded with Rory McIlroy. It appeared as if Woods was preparing for a possible return to competition at the 2026 Masters. He was ramping up his playing schedule after undergoing two surgeries in 2025: A procedure to repair a torn Achilles tendon in April, followed by a lumbar disc replacement surgery in October. It was his seventh back surgery.
